replying_to: Replying to Hopular: Modern Hopfield Networks for Tabular Data
display_title: Official Review of Paper1505 by Reviewer 6m2C

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper presents a new deep learning architecture, Hopular, for tabular dataset classification problems with a relatively small number of samples (mostly lower than 1000). These problems are commonly solved by classical machine-learning methods, but there were several recent papers on trying to solve them with deep learning. The new proposed architecture is based on a Hopfield module, which enables access to the original training data in each layer of the network. 
The performance of the new network is evaluated on 16 datasets from a previously published paper, and compared with 26 other modeling methods. It reached the best performance with average rank of 6.75, while the next best method (SVM) had an average rank of 8.25. Next, Hopular was compared with XGBoost and NPT on 4 larger datasets (~10K samples) from another previously published paper. Hopular was again better in terms of average rank (1.5 vs. 2). Additionally, the inference time of Hopular was similar to XGBoost, even though the training time of Hopular was 20x longer.
content.main_review:
This paper considers an important problem and suggests an interesting architecture. However, the experimental analysis provided raises several concerns:
-	Selecting only some of the datasets used in each of the two referenced papers may raise the concern that the results were not representative enough. Even though the authors had various reasons for their selection, it would be better to provide the results for the same datasets as in the referenced papers, at least for one of the papers.
-	The hyperparameter tuning of the models in the first comparison is not detailed, and it is unclear which hyperparameters were tuned and whether the same number of hyperparameter iterations were done for Hopular and the other models. Rather than comparing to many models that might not be well-tuned, it would be better to compare to one or two well-tuned popular models, e.g., XGBoost and CatBoost. The tuning should include at least the key hyperparameters (e.g., in XGBoost the number of trees ranging between 10 and 1000 and their depth ranging between 1 and 20). It should perform the same number of iterations for each model, e.g., 100 or 1000 iterations with a standard Bayesian optimization package. Also, while providing ranks makes the presentation clearer, the authors should also provide the 
actual results of their runs, including standard error, as they did for the second paper, to enable a better impression of the results.
-	In the second comparison, the XGBoost results of the referenced paper were not reproduced, so the validity of the results is unclear. It should again be clarified how many hyperparameter optimization iterations were done, how many trees, which depths, etc.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper presents interesting technical contributions for an important problem. However, the experimental evaluation was not done rigorously enough to support the main conclusion. It is unclear if different models had a different number of hyperparameter tuning iterations, and if the tuned hyperparameters and ranges were the most important ones. I therefore recommend rejecting this paper in its present form. I would be willing to reconsider if the authors provide the required data along the lines described above (even if the updated results would show a smaller improvement, its significance and soundness could be higher).

content.title: Response to Reviewer 6m2C
content.comment:
Thank you for your insightful review!

**Regarding point 1**

Deep Learning lacks behind its expectations especially on small tabular datasets. This is why we primarily tested Hopular’s performance on these small-sized UCI datasets. A more detailed description of the dataset selection process can be found in the paper on page 7, “Datasets.”. Traditional Machine Learning methods like XGBoost (Chen & Guestrin, 2016) often outperform Deep Learning methods on small- and medium-sized tabular datasets. This is the reason we selected the datasets of (Shwartz-Ziv & Armon, 2021), where XGBoost performed better than Deep Learning methods that have been designed for tabular data. These were the four smallest datasets of (Shwartz-Ziv & Armon, 2021).

**Regarding point 2**

Only Hopular, NPT and XGBoost have been tuned by us for the small-sized datasets. The remaining methods were already tuned in (Wainberg et al., 2016) and (Klambauer et al., 2017). NPTs and Hopulars hyperparameters were chosen in accordance with (Kossen et al., 2021), and are listed and described in subsection A1. XGBoost was tuned according to (Shwartz-Ziv & Armon, 2021), as it is described for the medium-sized datasets. Here, it is tuned for the number of trees, depth, and a vast number of additional hyperparameters by the Bayseian hyperparameter optimization package “Hyperopt”. For XGBoost we performed 1000 hyperparameter runs on each datasets. For the Deep Learning methods only 24 hyperparameter settings were performed since training time is longer for each run compared to XGBoost.  Thank you for pointing this out, we agree that this description is missing for the small-sized datasets. Thank you for your suggestion, we will be more explicit about the respective results in the updated version.

**Regarding point 3**

We used the same Bayesian hyperparameter optimization procedure as well as the same hyperparameter ranges as described in Appendix C by (Shwartz-Ziv & Armon, 2021). The corresponding hyperparameter ranges can be found in subsection C.2 of (Shwartz-Ziv & Armon, 2021). The optimization package of choice, in accordance with (Shwartz-Ziv & Armon, 2021), was <hyperopt> (Bergstra et al., 2013). As this package changed the default loss type in version 1.3.0, we include the new loss type as well as the old one in Table 2 and Table 3, respectively. We refer to the specific hyperparameter ranges as well as the chosen optimization procedure in subsection 4.2 in “Hyperparameter Selection” as well as at the end of this subsection, where we reference Table 2 and Table 3. For XGBoost (Chen & Guestrin, 2016), we evaluated 1000 hyperparameter settings with 1000 estimators (gradient boosting rounds) each. We agree that we were not able to reproduce the results as reported by (Shwartz-Ziv & Armon, 2021). We aim to be more explicit about this and include the hyperparameter ranges as well as additional information about the Bayesian hyperparameter optimization procedure in the updated version.

replying_to: Replying to Hopular: Modern Hopfield Networks for Tabular Data
display_title: Official Review of Paper1505 by Reviewer wdX3

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes "Hopular" a model for prediction on small tabular datasets based on "modern hopfield networks".
Modern hopfield networks, as presented in this paper, are equivalent to multihead self-attention (MHSA).
"Hopular" stacks multiple Hopular blocks. 
Each Hopular block contains two hopfield modules: the first module applies MHSA between different samples. The second module applies MHSA between different features of the same sample (This is shared/parallelised over all samples).
The draft shows superior performance of Hopular in small-to-medium large tabular data settings.
content.main_review:
## Strength

The introduction gives an excellent overview over recent developments in the field of machine learning models for tabular data.
The paper is overall well-written and, overall, a pleasant read.

## Weaknesses

I have two main concerns about this submission, which I detail below.

### Novelty of Hopular

I do not see how Hopular provides much algorithmic novelty, except for framing NPTs/SAINT in the language of modern Hopfield networks.

As the authors themselves write, modern Hopfield networks are equivalent to attention. As they do not write, Eq. 8 of this paper is, as far as I can tell, almost exactly equal to multi-head self-attention. (There is a slight difference in how skip connections are handled.)

As mentioned above, each Hopular block contains two Hopfield modules: one performing MHSA between samples, and another performing MHSA between features.
For the MHSA between samples, the input is reshaped from $n \times d \times e$ to $n \times d \cdot e$.
This is exactly identical to how SAINT and NPTs construct their basic building blocks.
(SAINT does not explore more than one "Hopular block" in their paper, but Kossen et al. do in fact employ this for NPTs.)

The similarities, particularly to NPTs do not end here:
* The input embeddings are performed identically to NPTs.
* The masking mechanism, with stochastic masks applied to both input labels and input features, is identical.
* The loss is a convex combination of supervised label and feature masking loss for both Hopular and NPTs. Hopular also use the cosine schedule from Kossen et al. to anneal this.
* The same optimizer is used for Hopular and NPTs.
* The output layer is, as far as I can tell, identical.
* Hopular even makes use of the hyperparameters, optimisers, and training schedule used by NPTs.

As far as I can tell, Hopular and NPTs are almost functionally identical.
Unfortunately, many of the above similarities are not mentioned by the authors. 
Instead the authors focus on two differences between Hopular and NPTs: (1) a scaling factor $\beta$ in the self-attention mechanism, and (2) the fact that "the original training set and the original input are provided at each layer" in Hopular.
Given all all these similarities, I can't help but wonder: Are the authors perhaps building Hopular on top of the open-source NPT implementation?

**(1) The Scaling Factor.** In S.3 the authors claim that experiments in S.4 confirm that a large $\beta$ value improves predictions for Hopular. However, I cannot find any information on $\beta$ in the experiments. Can you provide an ablation where you fix $\beta=1$ in Hopular and show this degrades performance? So far, I am not convinced that the introduction of $\beta$ is beneficial.


**(2) Original Training Set/Input at each layer.** The authors claim that only Hopular has the original training set/input available at each layer. While this is technically true,  I feel that the difference to NPTs/SAINT is exaggerated.
Both SAINT and NPTs use MHSA with *skip connections* (cf. e.g. Eqs. (2-4) in the NPT paper).
Therefore, while the original input is not passed to directly each layer, it is still easy for the model to preserve information from the input or to ignore layers if needed.
And given that the task for NPTs/SAINT/Hopular is predicting masked values, it seems to me that the input getting iteratively refined (as done through the skip connections in NPTs/SAINT) is sensible, and I do not see inherent value for presenting the original training set/input to each layer.
Can you provide an ablation where you use standard MHSA skip connections, showing that your "input-skip connections" perform better?
Hopular with MHSA style skip connections is entirely identical to NPTs, right?



I would welcome a revision to this paper that more fairly represents the similarities of Hopular and prior work.
The current draft feels too much like it's trying to hide these similarities – especially to NPTs.
Additionally, clarifying any differences to NPTs (are there any in addition to skip connections + $\beta$) would be helpful.


### Experimental Results – Selection of Datasets and Tuning of Baselines

The authors compare Hopular for a relatively large selection of datasets and baselines.
Unfortunately, I feel there are a variety of shortcomings that the authors should address in order to provide further credibility to their results.
I've highlighted points of particular importance to me in bold.

* **Why are LightGBM and Catboost not implemented as baselines?** Easy to use open source implementations (with SKLearn interface) for these models exist, and they perform strongly and so should be included here. (You seem to be aware that these are important baselines as well.) Both models performed highly competitively when SAINT/NPT compared against them.
* "For NPT we use the hyperparameters reported in (Kossen et al., 2021), which also form the basis of Hopular’s hyperparameter selection process" -->  **This sounds like you only tune hyperparameters for Hopular but not for NPTs?** It would be unfair to tune hyperparameters for one model only and not for the other. Further, Kossen et al. use different sets of hyperparameters for different dataset sizes.  (And they sweep over a selection of configurations in the small data setting.) Which of these hyperparameters did you use? **The fact that NPTs perform rather well for the medium data setting makes me think you might have used only their medium-large hyperparameter configuration and not the 'small' configuration that they recommend for small datasets**. I also don't quite understand table A.1. Again, it sounds like these are hyperparameters searched only for Hopular?
* In general, I appreciate the idea of selecting datasets that are "hard" for neural network models. However, are results over "normal" datasets not also important? Further, **presenting results for some of the datasets from NPTs or SAINT would provide further credibility to your results** (can you recreate their results?) as well as provide some credibility to the NPT/SAINT papers (is it possible to recreate their results)? **Given the similarities in architecture design between Hopular and NPTs, it is unclear to me why Hopular would perform so much better than NPTs.**
* Can you demonstrate that Hopular actually relies on sample-sample attention mechanism for prediction? Or is this just learning to predict in parametric fashion, ignoring all sample-sample relations?
* Relatedly: A lot of the motivation of the paper has to do with the 'storing capacity of modern Hopfield' networks. Can you show that the the Hopfield modules do in fact learn to store input data? Why would they learn to store input data if the training data is provided at each iteration?
* **It seems extremely odd that XGBoost performs almost as badly as Nearest Neighbors in the small data setting.** This is entirely unlike the performance reported in the SAINT/NPT papers, where XGBoost consistently performs near the top. Again, it would be nice to include some of their datasets to confirm that your hyperparameter optimisation/code is not at fault here. Note, that for NPTs this also includes small datasets with ~<1000 datapoints. Further, it seems that your hyperparameter tuning is different for the medium sized datasets, where now XGBoost performs rather competitively.
* Can you release details of the XGBoost hyperparameter tuning for both scenarios? You write that " More details about the hyperparameter selection and the precise hyperparameter settings can be found in the Appendix Table A1" but no details about XGBoost are given there.
* All datasets you report are classification. Is there a reason for not showing results on regression datasets? I know regression datasets of matching size exist in UCI (e.g. Protein, Concrete, Boston Housing, Yacht).
* Can you provide mean rank in addition to median rank? Can you please also provide quantiles/standard deviations of the median/mean rank? Also, please provide the individual numbers of all methods on all datasets as well.
* The provided runtime/step statistic in Table 4 seems somewhat irrelevant for model training. I assume XGBoost and Hopular need a different number of steps for training to converge? (And I assume gradient-based Hopular needs much more steps.)
* Do you tune hyperparameters on a validation set? This may sound obvious, but I have previously reviewed papers that did not do this, and so I would welcome you to add information about training/validation and test set sizes.
* It would be great if you could release the code before the end of the reviewing period. It does not seem helpful to release it shortly after.


## Small Comments

* "In real world, however, most machine learning applications face tabular data with less than 10,000 samples." While plausible, this claim requires a citation or evidence to be backed up. Especially if it's part of the abstract.
* " For small-sized and medium-sized tabular data, these methods dominate real world applications." While plausible, this claim requires a citation or evidence to be backed up.
* The introduction of modern hopfield networks (with recounted theorems) is nice, but why is it necessary? (Especially if all of this is equivalent to MHSA). The main purpose it seems to serve is to illustrate the storing capacity of modern Hopfield networks. However, it is unclear to me why I should be excited about the possibility of "storing a lot of data". (I can also store data in an array. Are Hopulars better at storing data than an array?) Also, regarding the last sentence of S.2: what dimensionality would be needed in theory to store the datasets you experiment with? Does this match up with the results?
* "Problematic datasets in (Klambauer et al., 2017) are characterized by having an accuracy range of 0.5 or higher across well established methods" What is an accuray range? Does this mean that the max - min performance of the investigated method in Klambauer et al. is  $\ge 0.5$?
* "One advantage of Hopular compared to XGBoost is the capability to handle data with missing values without the need for additional imputation techniques. This makes Hopular highly relevant for real world scenarios where incomplete data is a common companion." --> This is somewhat of a weird closing statement for this paper, given that both NPT and SAINT can do this just as well. Please clarify how Hopular can do this better than SAINT/NPTs or remove. Missing data also is not discussed elsewhere in this paper, so I fail to see how this fits the "conclusion" section.


## Language

* "it failed to meet ~~its~~ expectations on tabular data" Deep learning does not have expectations, people have expectations *of* deep learning.
* "In real world, however, most machine learning applications [...]" --> "In *the* real word" or "In real-world settings"
* Inconsistent abbreviations for plural forms: "GBDT" but "SVMs". Why not "GBDTs"? (Specifically in "GBDT typically lead to higher [...]")
* " SAINT also uses self-supervised pre-training [...]. Non-Parametric Transformers (NPTs) also use feature self-attention and inter-sample attention" --> It is not 100% clear what the two "also"s refer to here. I would guess, that the first refers to both TabGNN and SAINT using self-supervised pre-training? (But NPTs also have a self-supervised component.) And the second "also" refers to both SAINT and NPTs having two self-attention mechanisms: one between features and one between samples? Maybe it would be more clear to specify this directly?
content.summary_of_the_review:
I hope the authors engage with my review during the rebuttal period.
I look forward to a lively discussion, and hope the authors address as many of the concerns raised in above.

My main objections to accepting this paper in its current state are 
* remaining unclearness in pitching the novelty of Hopular in relation to NPTs/SAINT – Hopular is much more similar than what, I feel, the reader is led to believe. 
* that the current draft does not ablate the effect of Hopulars main novelties: changing the MHSA skip connection from layer-to-layer to input-to-layer as well as introducing the $\beta$ scaling factor. It seems surprising to me that these changes would increase performance of Hopular over NPT by such a margin in the small data setting.
* the open questions wrt to the experimental evalution. In particular: the missing LightGBM/CatBoost baselines, missing details for hyperparameter tuning for XGBoost, potentially wrong hyperparameter tuning / no tuning for NPTs, missing results on datasets used in SAINT/NPTs, explanation of surprisingly bad XGBoost results. A code release before the end of the review period would be great as well, given that this will erase any doubt about the procedures.

If the authors engage and clarify a significant number of my concerns, I will raise my score.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1505 by Reviewer wdX3

content.title: Response to Reviewer wdX3
content.comment:
Thank you for your insightful review!

**Regarding novelty of Hopular**

Self-attention, as introduced in (Vaswani et al., 2017), is a special case of a modern Hopfield network for Deep Learning architectures (Ramsauer et al., 2020), in which the input is attended to itself. Modern Hopfield networks access an external memory in a content-based fashion. This enables Deep Learning architectures equipped with modern Hopfield networks to incorporate virtually any external data source as long as each individual datum is representable as a real vector. Hopular populates this external memory in two different ways: (i) $H_s$ uses the training set as an external memory, whereas (ii) $H_f$ uses the embedded feature representations of the original input sample as an external memory. This is the huge advantage of Hopular, as this enables the current prediction to be refined layer per layer – like standard iterative learning algorithms. Hopular does not make use of multi-head self-attention (Vaswani et al., 2017), as the current input of a layer is never attended to itself.

It is not guaranteed that an architecture with MHSA and residual connections learns to pass the original data through the network in a manner that fulfills this condition. Further, the network would need to store this information in its parameters which would require a substantial number of parameters only for storing data. The number of parameters needed to store datasets will grow proportionally to the dataset sizes

Hopular is most closely related to NPT (Kossen et al., 2021) and SAINT (Somepalli et al., 2021), which we found during our literature research. We openly show this connection e.g. on page 3, first paragraph. Some similarities are natural, like using BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) or LAMB (You et al., 2020), as the corresponding methods can be seen as being state of the art in the domain of attention-based architectures. For others, like the Lookahead optimizer wrapper (Zhang et al., 2019), we were indeed inspired by (Kossen et al., 2021). We will add this source of inspiration in the updated version.

**Regarding input embeddings**

Embedding input features independently to each other was already employed by previous publications like AutoInt (Song et al., 2019) for discrete as well as continuous features. Adding a positional encoding, is commonly used in attention-based architectures, and was already used by (Vaswani et al., 2017). We followed (Song et al., 2019) for the feature embeddings and (Devlin et al., 2019) for the positional embeddings. The feature type embedding is a natural extension of the segment embedding of (Devlin et al., 2019). To the best of our knowledge, NPT (Kossen et al., 2021) was the first method to embed the feature types in a similar way. We aim to more explicitly describe the input embedding in the updated version.

**Regarding masking**

We are using the same masking procedure as in BERT (Devlin et al., 2019). NPT excludes the probability of replacing a token/attribute with the unchanged version of itself – this is exactly the same setting as (Devlin et al., 2019) discussed in Appendix C.2, Table 8. We aim to describe the masking procedure more explicitly in the updated version.

**Regarding hyperparameters**

Yes, we state this in the paper in subsection 4.1, “Hyperparameter Selection:” as well as in subsection A.1. To emphasize the impact of the Hopfield modules, we kept the same hyperparameters as were found by (Kossen et al., 2021). This way, the performance differences can be more clearly attributed toward these architectural differences.

**Regarding similarities**

We explicitly mention the similarities between NPT and our method, exemplarily: (i) page 3, top paragraph – “Hopular is most closely related to SAINT (Somepalli et al., 2021) and Non-Parametric Transformers (NPTs) (Kossen et al., 2021) [...]”. (ii) page 6, “Feature Masking.” – “We follow state-of-the-art Deep Learning methods like SAINT (Somepalli et al., 2021) and Non-Parametric Transformers (NPTs) (Kossen et al., 2021) [...]”. (iii) page 6, “Hyperparameter Selection.” – “For NPT we use the hyperparameters reported in (Kossen et al., 2021) [...]”. After mentioning the similarities between NPT and Hopular on multiple occasions in the main paper as well as the Appendix, it only seems natural to set the focus on the differences.

**Regarding scaling factor**

In the Appendix, A.1, we wrote “As Hopular provides an additional adjustable scaling factor for $\beta$, we also tested scaling factors of 100 and 1000 [...]”. Table A1 specifies the corresponding hyperparameter settings. The role of $\beta$ in modern Hopfield networks for Deep Learning architectures is already described in (Ramsauer et al., 2020), Figure A.1. We will more explicitly report the impact of $\beta$ on Hopular’s performance in the updated version.

**Regarding minor comments**

Thank you for your suggestions, we will include them where appropriate.

content.title: Response to Reviewer wdX3
content.comment:
> It would be great if you could address the remaining points under "Experimental Results – Selection of Datasets and Tuning of Baselines".

**Regarding LightGBM and CatBoost**

We chose XGBoost as the GBDT implementation of choice, as it, according to (Shwartz-Ziv & Armon, 2021), usually outperforms Deep Learning based methods. Moreover, the hyperparameters of XGBoost were nonetheless optimized for each of the datasets separately, so we suspect only minor differences between different GBDT implementations. But we agree that using more than one GBDT implementation for a comparison, could further strengthen the position of our method. Thank you for this suggestion, we aim to extend the list of GBDT implementations by LightGBM and CatBoost.

**Regarding hyperparameter tuning**

For a fair comparison, we used the same hyperparameter settings for NPT as well as Hopular. They are described in subsection C.1.2 “Small Data Sweep” in (Kossen et al., 2021). Due to memory constraints (when working with the medium-sized datasets), we set the feature embedding size to 32 per feature. This is in accordance with (Kossen et al., 2021), subsection C.1.2, “Base Hyperparameter Configurations.”. As Hopular introduces, compared to e.g. NPT, an additional hyperparameter $\beta$, we repeated this set of hyperparameter settings two times, each with a different value for $\beta$. At Table A1 we state “Settings with a scaling factor of 1 were additionally performed for NPT.”, so Table A1 lists the hyperparameters for Hopular as well as NPT. We aim to more explicitly describe the hyperparameter optimization procedure in the updated version.

**Regarding datasets**

We focused on “hard” datasets only – i.e. small- and medium-sized datasets – as Deep Learning methods are considered state-of-the-art when working with “normal” datasets – i.e. large-sized datasets. Moreover, we selected the datasets of (Shwartz-Ziv & Armon, 2021), where XGBoost performed better than Deep Learning methods that have been designed for tabular data. These were the four smallest datasets of (Shwartz-Ziv & Armon, 2021), so one could call them “hard” datasets as well. Hopular’s performance is mainly driven by modern Hopfield networks for Deep Learning architectures (Ramsauer et al., 2020). This enables Hopular to incorporate and access external memories in a content-based fashion. This is the huge advantage of Hopular, as accessing the training set as well as the original embedded feature representation of the input sample enables the current prediction to be refined layer per layer – like standard iterative learning algorithms.

**Regarding storage capacity**

The Hopfield modules do not need to learn to store the input data themselves. This is the huge advantage of modern Hopfield networks, they are able to access external data in a content-addressable way. As stated above, Hopular populates this external memory in two ways: (i) $H_s$ uses the training set as an external memory, whereas (ii) $H_f$ uses the embedded feature representations of the original input sample as an external memory. Consequently, there is no need for the Hopfield modules to learn to store the input/training data, as they are already present in the memory by design. Hence, not the content of the memory itself, but the access to (the retrieval from) this memory is learned. This retrieval is done in a content-addressable way, whereas the type of fixed point of the modern Hopfield network specifies the type of retrieved pattern – as exemplarily depicted in Figure A1 in (Ramsauer et al., 2020).

**Regarding XGBoost**

XGBoost was tuned according to (Shwartz-Ziv & Armon, 2021), as it is described for the medium-sized datasets. Thank you for pointing this out, we agree that this description is missing for the small-sized datasets. You are right, XGBoost performs rather competitively on medium-sized datasets. This is consistent with the results in SAINT (Somepalli et al., 2021) and NPT (Kossen et al., 2021), where most datasets would not fit into our small-sized dataset category. We aim to more thoroughly investigate these performance differences in the updated version.

**Regarding dataset type**

For a fair comparison of Hopular with the methods discussed in (Klambauer et al., 2017), we chose our datasets accordingly. The specific dataset selection procedure is discussed in the paper on page 7, “Datasets.”. This selection procedure resulted in the exclusion of all small regression datasets. Thank you for your suggestion, we will aim for more heterogeneous datasets in the updated version.

**Regarding validation set**

Yes, we tune the hyperparameters on the respective validation sets. Concerning details on train/test splits we wrote in the paper on page 6, second paragraph – “The datasets and train/test splits were taken from (Fernández-Delgado et al., 2014).” For medium-sized datasets we used train/val/test set sizes according to (Shwartz-Ziv & Armon, 2021).

content.title: Reviewer Response
content.comment:
Thank you for your reply.

I look forward to seeing the updated version that incorporates the changes you mention. 
I do find the Hopular more interesting now then after my initial review.

However, I still feel that the current draft gives a somewhat unclear account of what the novelties of Hopular are.
Further, the changes you promise to the experimental results/setup sound good but have not been implemented.
Similar to Reviewer 6m2C, it is not clear to me why not at least some of  these changes have not been implemented (prior to the deadline for updates).
Therefore, I don't feel comfortable adjusting my score to near-accept just yet.
(Code availability/reproducibility would also help this submission.)
I can imagine that a resubmission of this work with these changes implemented will fit the bar for acceptance.

content.title: Response to Reviewer wdX3
content.comment:
Thank you for your follow-up comments and questions.

> If I understand correctly, the current input is however used as the "key" matrix in self-attention, correct?

Both Hopfield modules access an external memory in a content-based fashion: (i) $H_s$ uses the training set as an external memory, whereas (ii) $H_f$ uses the embedded feature representations of the original input sample as an external memory. Using the terminology of (Vaswani et al., 2017), the external memory of Hopular may be seen as the “keys” and “value” matrices in self-attention. But we want to emphasize that self-attention is **not** part of Hopular’s architecture, as the current input, the “query” in (Vaswani et al., 2017), is never attended to itself.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a deep learning approach for tabular data that uses modern Hopfield networks. This new architecture aims to generalizes better than XGBoost on tabular data with less than 10000 examples. The approach is interesting and it shows better generalization performance than XGBoost and other deep learning approaches for some datasets. The main difference between the proposed approach and the closest deep learning architectures is that the proposed solution uses the full training dataset as input to each layer of the network. In my opinion, the paper can be highly improved in terms of technical clarity and experimental results. More details are provided in the main review.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
+ Useful survey of the related work in the field of deep learning for tabular data
+ First attempt to use Hopfield networks for deep learning architectures for tabular data (use the whole dataset as input to each network layer)
+ Interesting first results when compared to XGBoost in terms of generalization performance

Weaknesses:
- Section 3 should include a top-level diagram that describes the full architecture with Hopfield modules and blocks. In the current state, it is difficult to understand how the actual proposed architecture looks like (incl. the full set of model hyper-parameters).
- The experimental section could be highly improved to make the contributions of the paper stronger. Here are a few suggestions: 
    1) In general there is no GBDT implementation (XGBoost/LightGBM/CatBoost) that works best on all datasets. Thus, especially on these new datasets studied in the paper, the authors could also include the results for LightGBM/CatBoost (accuracy and runtime) if available. It would also be interesting to see how a differentiable neural network would compare to the proposed approach (e.g., NODE).
    2) Please provide details about the hardware setup used for the experiments.
    3) The hyper-parameter optimization is not clear in the paper. E.g., all the models shown in Table 1 have been tuned? What hyper-parameters have been tuned and what ranges have been used for the hyper-parameters? What tools have been used to tune the models? It is only mentioned for XGBoost, but even for XGBoost there are no further details provided.
    4) How many train/test splits have been used? Was (nested) cross-validation used? Please provide more details. This is very important especially when dealing with small datasets, special attention is required when evaluating the model quality on such datasets. 
    5) In section 4.2, are the default hyper-parameters used or the tuned ones?
    6) The results in Tables 2/3 show that the test accuracy on the datasets on which Hopfield wins against XGBoost is extremely close to the NPT accuracy. Could you please provide information about the training time of NPT?
    7) At least the results in Tables 2/3 should include a statistical significance analysis (currently this is missing).
    8) Section 4.3: what is the meaning of a step for XGBoost? Is this runtime the total runtime of the training routine? Could you please provide the runtime for all the datasets under study?
    9) Section 4.3: please report the NPT runtime as well.
   10) To make the paper stronger, I would increase the number of baselines (e.g., other GBDT frameworks, differentiable neural networks etc) for which I would report the test accuracy and the runtimes.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper has the potential to bring a very good contribution to the field of deep learning architectures for tabular data. However the paper in the current state requires quite a few improvements especially in terms of technical clarity and experimental results. Please see the main review section for more details.

content.title: Response to Reviewer wQkj
content.comment:
Thank you for your insightful review!

**Regarding architecture diagram**

Thank you for your suggestion. We aim to extend and improve the readability of the diagrams.

**Regarding point 1**

We chose XGBoost as the GBDT implementation of choice, as it, according to (Shwartz-Ziv & Armon, 2021), usually outperforms Deep Learning based methods. Moreover, the hyperparameters of XGBoost were nonetheless optimized for each of the datasets separately, so we suspect only minor differences between different GBDT implementations. But we agree that using more than one GBDT implementation for a comparison could further strengthen the position of our method. Thank you for the suggestion, we aim to extend the list of GBDT implementations.

In Table 1 you can find eight Deep Learning methods that we used as baselines for small-sized datasets. For medium-sized datasets we used the Deep Learning method NPT as a benchmark architecture.

**Regarding point 2**

Since the medium-sized datasets have approximately 10K samples, and Hopular has access to the entire dataset at each layer, we used an 80 GB Nvidia A100 GPU for our experiments. A memory usage of 40 GB is only exceeded for the largest dataset in combination with the largest architecture setting. For the small-sized datasets, a memory of approximately 10 GB suffices.

**Regarding point 3**

Only Hopular, NPT and XGBoost have been tuned by us for the small-sized datasets. The remaining methods were already tuned in (Wainberg et al., 2016) and (Klambauer et al., 2017). NPT’s and Hopular’s hyperparameters were chosen in accordance with (Kossen et al., 2021), and are listed and described in subsection A1. XGBoost was tuned according to (Shwartz-Ziv & Armon, 2021), as it is described for the medium-sized datasets. Thank you for pointing this out, we agree that this description is missing for the small-sized datasets. We will include a more detailed description in the updated version.

**Regarding point 4**

Concerning details on train/test splits, we wrote in the paper on page 6, second paragraph – “The datasets and train/test splits were taken from (Fernández-Delgado et al., 2014).” For medium-sized datasets we used train/val/test set sizes according to (Shwartz-Ziv & Armon, 2021).

**Regarding point 5**

We wrote in the paper, subsection 4.2, “Hyperparameter Selection.” – “We used the default hyperparameters for Hopular as well as NPT, which were found during the hyperparameter selection process for the UCI dataset in previous Subsection 4.1.”. So the default hyperparameters in subsection 4.2 are the result of the tuning process of subsection 4.1.

**Regarding point 6**

Thank you for pointing this out. Since the runtimes for Hopular and NPT are approximately equal, we did not explicitly report it. We will include this runtime information in the updated version.

**Regarding point 7**

Thank you for pointing this out. We will include the results of the statistical analysis in the updated version.

**Regarding point 8**

Table 4 shows the average total runtime of training XGBoost (Chen & Guestrin, 2016), whereas one step refers to one hyperparameter setting. We aim to include more elaborate runtime estimates in the updated version.

**Regarding point 9**

We plan to include details about NPT runtimes in the updated version.

**Regarding point 10**

Thank you for your comment. For small-sized datasets, we compare our method to 26 different baseline methods. We think this amount of comparisons is sufficient for an adequate method evaluation. For medium-sized datasets we will extend our baselines by LightGBM, CatBoost and others. We will include these additional experiments in the updated version and be more explicit about the respective results.

display_title: Official Review of Paper1505 by Reviewer ZM7R

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper uses modern Hopfield networks for dealing with tabular data.  The proposed architecture has two Hopfield modules: one for memorizing the training dataset, and the other one for embedded input features. The architecture is evaluated on small and medium size datasets,  good performance is achieved.
content.main_review:
This is a nice paper that explores a novel architecture that may benefit from memorizing a (small) tabular dataset. I like the overall idea, and the authors seem to report strong empirical results. Certain parts of the paper are however confusing and somewhat misleading. I will explain these issues below. 

1.  I understand the construction of the module $H_s$, which memories the training set. By the way, is the parameter $n$ - the size of the training set? It seems to be undefined in the manuscript. I am having troubles understanding the role of $H_f$. Specifically, what is the matrix of memories $Y$? Is it a set of learnable parameters, or does it depend on the inputs $\Xi$ in some way? 

2. In equation 8, the authors state that they can use $N$ Hopfield networks inside $H_s$. What is the difference between these networks? It seems that the memory matrix $X$ is the same in all of them. Are they different because the matrices $W$ are different, or are matrices $W$ also equal in all those Hopfield networks? 

3. The presentation of the modern Hopfield networks is somewhat skewed toward the formulation by Ramsauer et al. and largely ignores the original formulation by Krotov and Hopfield (except for mentioning it once on page 3).  The authors have a right to work with any formulation, but they should cite the original work when they introduce the concept for the first time (page 2). The authors should also cite the paper by Krotov and Hopfield from ICLR 2021 (https://openreview.net/forum?id=X4y_10OX-hX), which provides a neat derivation of the energy function and update rules that they are using. 

4. I understand that the authors are focusing on small datasets (which is fine), but I am wondering about how would their approach scale with increasing the size of the dataset? For instance it seems that the size of the memory matrix X should grow linearly with the size of the training set. Even for medium size datasets, 10k instances, it’s already a sizable matrix. What is the reason why the authors do not apply their approach to large tables, say millions of instances? Is it because there is a computational reason that their architecture leads to worse accuracies than the more traditional approaches; or is it because their network doesn’t fit into the memory, but if it did it would also likely work well? 

5. Could the authors please provide the values of the hyperparameters, such as $e$, $d$, and $h$? It is hard to assess the scalability of their approach even qualitatively without at least a ballpark for these parameters.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I like the approach and the paper in general. If the authors can answer my questions and address the issues above I am happy to increase my scores.

content.title: Response to Reviewer ZM7R
content.comment:
Thank you for your insightful review!

**Regarding point 1**

Thanks for pointing this out, we now explicitly define n. You are right, $n$ is the size of the dataset. The module $H_f$ identifies feature-feature interactions, where the matrix $\bf Y$ is the embedded representation of an original input sample. $H_f$ extracts the interactions of the features of the input sample. To explain $\bf Y$: (i) the original input sample has d features. (ii) Each of these $d$ features is mapped to a feature representation vector of dimension $e$. (iii) The feature representation vectors are combined to the matrix $\bf Y$, which therefore has dimension $e\times d$.

**Regarding point 2**

You are right, the matrices $\bf W$ are different for each Hopfield network, which enables each of them to specialize on a different task.

**Regarding point 3**

Yes, you are right. We should cite the original work.

The energy function of (Krotov & Hopfield, 2016) has already been presented in (Chen et al., 1986), in (Psaltis et al., 1986), in (Gardner, 1987) in Eq. (1), in (Abbot et al., 1987) in Eq. (3) and (4) but also Eq. (5), in (Baldi et al., 1987) in Eq. (1), in (Horn et al., 1988) in Eq. (3) and (4), in (Caputo et al., 2002) in Eq. (4) and (5) and (6).

The polynomial storage capacity proven in (Krotov & Hopfield, 2016) has already been proven in (Gardner, 1987) see Eq. (5), in (Abbot et al., 1987) see Eq. (22), in (Baldi et al., 1987) see equation directly before  "(3) Generalized spectral rule:", in (Horn et al., 1988) see Eq. (12), in (Caputo et al., 2002) see Eq. (21).

The update rule in (Krotov & Hopfield, 2016) has already been used also by (Baldi et al., 1987) in Eq. (2). This update rule, which is the difference of energies, has been known for a long time as a zero-temperature Monte Carlo dynamics or as a zero-temperature Glauber dynamics.

In (Caputo et al., 2002) an energy function has been used, which replaces the polynomial in the energy function by an exponential as in (Demircigil et al., 2017).

To follow the suggestion of the reviewer, we will cite all this original work in the new version.

_References:_

Chen et al. High order correlation model for associative memory. AIP Conference Proceedings 151, 86,  1986

Psaltis et al. Nonlinear discriminant functions for associative memories. AIP Conference Proceedings 151, 370, 1986

P. Baldi and S. S. Venkatesh. Number of stable points for spin-glasses and neural networks of higher orders. Phys. Rev. Lett., 58:913-916, 1987

E. Gardner. Multi-connected neural network models. J. of Phys A, 20(11):3453-3464, 1987

L. F. Abbott and Y. Arian. Storage capacity of generalized networks. Phys. Rev. A, 36:5091-5094, 1987

D. Horn and M. Usher. Capacities of multiconnected memory models. J. Phys. France, 49(3): 389-395, 1988

B. Caputo and H. Niemann. Storage capacity of kernel associative memories. In Proceedings of the International Conference on Artificial Neural Networks (ICANN), pp. 51-56, 2002

**Regarding point 4**

The computational complexity for training grows quadratically with the size of the training set. Each training sample is used as an initial state for the Hopfield network which stores the whole training set. For smaller training set sizes, this can be parallelized using a GPU. For larger training set sizes, this is infeasible. Yes, we also believe that Hopular would work well for large datasets.

Over and above that, our primary goal is to test Hopular on small- and medium-sized datasets on which classical Machine Learning methods like GBDT excel.

**Regarding point 5**

We set $e = 32$, since NPT uses this setting for datasets with a decent amount of attributes. Because $h = e * d / N$, we have two different values per dataset for $h$: (i) one for $N = 8$ and (ii) one of $N = 16$ modern Hopfield networks. Thank you for pointing this out, we will clarify this in the updated version.

content.title: Response to all reviewers
content.comment:
We want to thank all reviewers for their time and valuable suggestions.

We were pleased to see that reviewers found the paper and the therein presented architecture interesting. We appreciate the thoughtful comments and suggested ideas of the reviewers. Unfortunately, this is not realizable within the time frame of the rebuttal. We distilled four main suggestions for improvement: (i) conducting ablation studies, especially in connection with $\beta$, (ii) adding further datasets, (iii) including more baselines, and (iv) clarifying the role of modern Hopfield networks for Deep Learning architectures in Hopular. We will include these suggestions to further strengthen the results of our paper.

We again would like to thank all reviewers for their time, insights and the overall high quality of the reviews.
